speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST OP TORONTO CITY COUNCIL FOR BAN ON IMPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Is it a fact that Toronto city council has requested the Minister of Justice to take steps to ban the importation of certain stilettos, or spring knives, on the ground that such stilettos or knives are offensive weapons and not likely to serve any useful purpose? What action, if any, has been taken by the government in connection with the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST OP TORONTO CITY COUNCIL FOR BAN ON IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his question. The answer to the first question is yes. As to the second question, I think that having regard to the fact that the request came as a letter from the city clerk of Toronto, I should simply read into the record the reply which I sent to that gentleman. My letter to him reads as follows:
Thank you for your letter of March 8 advising me that your city council at its meeting held on March 6, 1950, decided to request us to consider the placing of a ban on the importation of "spring knives or stilettos" on the grounds that they are considered offensive weapons.
I understand that what you are referring to by the term "spring knife or stiletto" is an article which is known as a spring stiletto. This weapon is similar to a spring knife except that it has no cutting edge, the blade when open being 31 to 4 inches in length. Mr. L. H. Taylor, the secretary of customs, informs us that stilettos are refused entry into Canada by virtue of an order in council passed under the Customs Act prohibiting the importation of certain offensive weapons without a permit, and no permit is given for stilettos, including stilettos of the spring type such as the one referred to in your letter.

I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence of which I have given him notice. In view of today's press reports, quoting a statement of the Minister of National Defence in regard to

the new four-engine prototype transport aircraft which is to be delivered shortly to the Royal Canadian Air Force, will the minister inform the House of Commons as to the date on which the Canadian Commercial Corporation was advised that the Royal Canadian Air Force required this aircraft?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):

speechtext:
As the leader of the opposition has said, he was good enough to give me notice of the question, but I happened to be at a meeting until a very late hour this morning, and I was not able to obtain the information that he desires. However, I can tell him that this aircraft was ordered to replace a North Star aircraft that was lent to Trans-Canada Air Lines, in consideration of a rent, in June, 1947. That aircraft was destroyed while in operation with T.C.A. on August 12, 1948. There was only one possible source from which to replace the aircraft, namely, Canadair Limited, from which it had been obtained, and which had the jigs and designs and so on. Negotiations continued steadily with regard to that aircraft. I have not been able to verify the exact date on which the Canadian Commercial Corporation was advised that we would want the aircraft replaced by Canadair, but certainly it would have been shortly after the date of destruction, because there was only one source of supply.
While I am speaking on this subject I should add that the press reports which appeared yesterday, and resulted in my making a release myself, follow an announcement which referred to this matter on May 18, 1949.

subtopic: A DELIVERY POINT UNDER INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANSWER TO QUESTION AS TO MAKING CHURCHILL
subtopic: A DELIVERY POINT UNDER INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) asked me a question with reference to the port of Churchill and its status as a basing point under the international wheat agreement. I have now obtained particulars from our representative at the international wheat conference in London. The port of Churchill is not a base point under the international wheat agreement, but arrangements have been made with the international wheat council that will enable Canada to utilize this port.
The arrangements are covered by resolutions passed at the twenty-third meeting of the executive committee held in London on January 31, 1950. The resolution adopted reads as follows:
That No. 1 Manitoba northern wheat in store port Churchill, Manitoba, be designated* a description* of wheat under article 6, paragraph 4, and that the advisory committee on price equivalents be requested to advise the executive committee on appropriate maximum and minimum price equivalents for such description of wheat, it being understood* that if Canada is requested to deliver wheat at maximum prices and/or if Canada requests importing countries to accept wheat at minimum prices the Fort William-Port Arthur prices basis should apply.
In accordance with this resolution Canada may negotiate and complete sales under1 the international wheat agreement for Churchill shipment at prices in line with c.i.f. prices at destination as compared with St. Lawrence shipment. If such sales can be made, Canada would secure the advantage of cheaper overall forwarding costs as the result of using this port. However, if Canada is called upon for wheat at the international wheat agreement maximum price or desires to put wheat at the international wheat agreement minimum price, we can only deliver wheat from Churchill at the Fort William-Port Arthur basic maximum or minimum prices as set out in the agreement.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, to provide that the act shall expire on the 30th day of April, 1951.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Explanation?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Now, or in committee?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill to be founded upon this resolution is a comparatively simple one. It will provide for the extension of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act until April 30, 1951-that is, for .thirteen months beyond the present expiry date.
While no other change is proposed, I should state that during the past year all the orders contained in the schedule to the act have been revoked except those relating to price and rent control. The government does not intend to invoke the limited powers now granted by the act to reimpose controls already lifted. Therefore the practical effect of the proposed bill is to continue the authority to control rentals only, for a further period. Thus we have arrived at the final stage in the difficult task of removing in an orderly way the controls introduced during the wartime emergency.
As the house is aware, the supreme court, by unanimous decision, has given its opinion that the wartime leasehold regulations are valid. I shall not refer at length to the reasons given by the distinguished members of the court in support of their opinion. I do wish, however, to draw particular attention to one general theme that is common to all of them, and for that purpose I shall quote from the opinion written by the chief justice:
There is no doubt that under normal conditions the subject matter of rents belongs to the provincial jurisdiction under the head of property and civil rights, in section 92 of the British North America Act. There is equally no doubt that under abnormal conditions, such as the existence of war, parliament may competently assume jurisdiction over rents. The fact is that, as a consequence of the last war, 1939-1945, parliament has taken over the control of rents. The Fort Frances case supra is authority for the proposition that, notwithstanding the cessation of hostilities, parliament is empowered to continue the control of rents for the purpose of concluding matters then pending, and of its discontinuance in an orderly manner, as the emergency permits, of measures adopted during and by reason of the emergency. It follows from the different orders in council and acts of parliament, recited in the order of reference, that the exceptional conditions brought about by war, which made the wartime leasehold regulations necessary, are still continuing, that the orderly transition from war to peace has not yet been completed, and that, in such circumstances, parliament is entitled and empowered to maintain such control as it finds necessary to ensure the orderly transition from war to peace. The judgments of the judicial committee of the privy council in the Fort Frances case supra and in Co-operative Committee on Japanese Canadians v. Attorney General for Canada (1947) A.C., 87, are conclusive on this point.
Transitional Measures Act
Then, after referring to the chemicals refer ence, the chief justice concluded:
In this instance, parliament has decided that the wartime leasehold regulations should be kept in force to a limited extent and to that extent, where necessary or advisable, to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace; and that, if they were abandoned abruptly and suddenly, unnecessary disruption would result.
There is nothing in the facts in the order of reference which would justify this court in deciding otherwise and thus supersede the opinion of parliament; and, in the circumstances, this court may not doubt that parliament may competently maintain the regulations it has adopted to meet the emergency and its continuance. Therefore, the wartime leasehold regulations are not ultra vires either in whole or in part.
With some differences in emphasis and point of view, all the other justices make the same point, that the court would require strong evidence, which was not forthcoming, to justify it in superseding the declared opinion of parliament.
While this unanimous opinion enables the government to proceed with confidence in asking parliament to renew the authority for rent control for a further period, it does not in any way alter the declared policy of the government to bring federal rent control to an end with the least possible delay. Time after time, and on every possible occasion, this policy has been made clear and, as the house will recall, fairly substantial further relaxation of rent control was in fact announced simultaneously with the reference to the supreme court.
The government considers that it should not ask parliament to continue its emergency authority any longer than is absolutely necessary. These are extraordinary powers and they should be exercised with great discretion. As the chief justice has said, "There is no doubt that under normal conditions the subject matter of rents belongs to the provincial jurisdiction under the head of property and civil rights, in section 92 of the British North America Act." The federal government has never disputed this, and has in fact, over the past two years, offered to vacate the field to any province that desired to assume responsibility; and one province, Saskatchewan, has already arranged to take over on April 1, 1950.
For these reasons, the government does not intend to ask for a further extension of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act beyond April 30, 1951. It is the government's view that over the next thirteen months the operation of the relaxations now in effect, combined with additions to the housing supply, will have permitted enough adjustment to take place so that any problem

Transitional Measures Act which may remain can be dealt with adequately-and with closer regard to local conditions and needs-on a provincial basis.
The house will appreciate that it is not usual for a government to give notice so long in advance as to its intentions respecting future legislation, but the government has decided to do so in this case in order that any province which may consider it desirable to assume some measure of rent control may have ample time to take such steps as may be deemed appropriate.
The date-April 30, 1951-has been selected because it coincides with the earliest expiration date of the leases entered into in return for the eighteen and twenty-two per cent increases permitted a few months ago. Incidentally, hon. members may be interested to learn that from reports of rental officials in the field it is estimated that seventy-five per cent of landlords of self-contained accommodation took advantage of the permission to obtain an increased rental in return for a lease expiring not earlier than April 30, 1951. Not all of their owners, of course, could or did raise rents to the full extent permitted. I mention this high percentage of leases because it shows that if the supreme court had found the federal regulations to be invalid, a very high proportion of tenants would have had secure tenure in their present dwellings for more than a year regardless of any action taken by the provinces.
Notwithstanding this further extension of federal rent control, I wish to make it perfectly clear, so that there can be no misunderstanding of the position, that the government does not now, nor has it at any time, disputed the right of any province to enact legislation dealing with rent control, and that it stands ready to withdraw the federal regulations in any province the government of which makes a formal request to that effect.
If any provincial government believes that it could administer rent control more equitably or more efficiently, the federal government will be pleased to withdraw its regulations in that province on a date to be fixed by the province, thus removing any possible conflict of laws. In addition, subject to parliamentary approval, the government is ready to continue its previous offer to pay the cost of provincial rent control for one year beginning not later than April 1, 1950, up to an amount equal to the cost of federal rent control in that province during a recent twelve-month period to be agreed upon.
Before I sit down, perhaps I should say a word as to the policy to be followed in the administration of rent control during the remaining thirteen months before the federal regulations finally expire. In previous years I


would have been most reluctant to say anything more than that the policy of orderly and gradual decontrol would be continued. Since only thirteen months remain, however, at the end of which time some provinces may wish to assume some measure of local rent control, it has been decided that no further adjustments will be made in rental ceilings or in the conditions affecting security of tenure, except in individual cases as permitted under the regulations as they now stand, or minor amendments to the regulations that may be found necessary. In short, there will be a standstill in rent control. The process of decontrol will, however, continue, as dwellings become vacant and thus free from con- ' trol and as landlords who have not already done so, take advantage of permission to enter into yearly leases in return for higher rents.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter now before the house relates not only to the principle of rent control but also to the way in which rent control will be carried on. The fact that the Supreme Court of Canada found that it is not ultra vires of the power of the Canadian parliament to exercise a continuing measure of rent control does not dispose of the question whether rent control can best be dealt with by arbitrary powers that are undefined, or by an act of the parliament of Canada which will clearly establish the legal rights of both tenants and landlords.
I do not think that many, if any, hon. members will seriously question the claim that during a state of emergency such as war there are many things that must be dealt with in a way that would not be acceptable in time of peace under our principles of parliamentary supremacy and responsible government. The fact that during a period of war emergency powers were invoked to cover a very wide field of activities of the people of Canada in their daily lives is no argument in favour of carrying that device forward into the years of peace, even though there is good reason to exercise controls over some of the same subject matters that were under consideration at that time.
During the war years and the years immediately after the war a wide measure of control was exercised by parliament and by the government as the executive branch of parliament. The Transitional Measures Act of 1947 was, as the name implies, intended to carry forward certain wartime controls through the transitional period from war to peace. Now we have reached the point where it is intended to carry forward only the controls over rent, the other emergency powers having been allowed to lapse. The question arises, then, whether the further

control of rents should be under emergency powers of this kind, or under an act of parliament which will state in clear and explicit terms exactly what the rights are of those who would be affected by its provisions.
This question is not being raised today for the first time. Last year the same measure was before the house. At that time there was some discussion relating to the course which would best meet our requirements, but the consideration which was given then did not relate to rent control alone. It related to the broader field of tbe transitional powers that were being carried forward at that time. The record will show we strongly urged that a bill should be introduced dealing with each of the subjects that the government of Canada thought should be dealt with under continuing measures of control. We pointed out that if the emergency powers could be carried forward in their existing form it was equally within the powers of parliament to enact legislation which would define the rights of those affected. It was contended that under the emergency powers the rights of tenants as well as landlords were not clearly defined, and that no one who would be affected by the continuing emergency powers could know definitely in advance what decision might be made.
On behalf of the party which I lead I urged a year ago that a bill should be introduced dealing with rent control, and that if such a bill were introduced it would receive the support of those sitting on this side of the house. I went so far as to express my own belief that a bill which properly defined the rights of tenants, landlords and all others affected, and provided a just measure of control, would receive the support of everyone in the house. Of course I was not in a position to speak on behalf of all hon. members. I still believe, however, that if a measure that fully protected the rights of tenants, landlords and all others concerned had been introduced at that time, it would have received support throughout the whole house.
Since that discussion took place a year ago we have received convincing evidence that there was reason to express concern about these loose and undefined powers exercised arbitrarily at the discretion of the government by order in council, without considering the views of members of parliament. I am not suggesting of course that the government exceeded the powers which were conferred upon it by the extension of the emergency powers dealt with under the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, which was extended last year. Then there was the substantial extension of rentals under the regulations which were announced in this house by
Transitional Measures Act the Minister of Finance last November. It will be recalled that at that time there was an increase of from twenty to twenty-five per cent in many rents, but the basic increase over a very broad field was twenty-two per cent. It is true that the increase was a pei-missive one, but it is also equally true that when landlords receive such permission it is in keeping with human nature that they should avail themselves of the invitation thus extended by the government. Whether there was any suggestion of justification or otherwise, that was the result. Therefore, by a measure which did not express the opinion of the house or of the parliament of Canada, rentals in Canada were greatly increased.
The war ended in 1945; this is 1950. There can be no reason for continuing rent control under arbitrary measures of this kind during the thirteen months which will be covered by the present extension suggested by the government. We certainly have now reached the stage of return to the ordinary peacetime procedure of parliament, when any measure of control affecting the daily lives of a large percentage of our people should be under a law of parliament enabling any Canadian to say: This is my right, and the courts of the land will protect me under that law. There is no sound argument in favour of the continuation of these emergency powers in this form. There is every argument in favour of the introduction, between now and the 31st of March, of a rent control bill which will deal fairly and justly with the rights of Canadians who will be affected by this legislation. I am confident that, entirely apart from any consideration of party point of view, any legislation which is just and affords proper protection to those affected, and which is enforceable by our courts under clearly defined terms, will receive the support of most members of the house.
If these emergency powers are extended in this way, there can be no assurance whatever that, without any advance knowledge on the part of hon. members who have been elected to carry on the business of the people of Canada, further orders may not be announced which will create additional hardship on many people throughout this country.

I was fully aware of what the ' minister said, but we have had too many examples of what can be done under those exceptions to be in any doubt as to whether or not the government would avail itself of them to the widest possible extent if in its discretion it decided it was wise to do so. That, after all, is not suggesting that the Minister of Finance is not seeking to convey to us in good faith his own appreciation of the situation. Without repeating to an extent that may seem to many hon, members an excessive return to the same subject, may I point out that a government that is able to stretch its conscience as it did in the suppression of the combines report is not a government that should be entrusted with this arbitrary power.
We have to remember that when these things are done we cannot even find out the basis on which that action is taken. To go back to the combines report, which establishes a pattern in other cases, we have to remember that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has informed us of those cases in which he received advice to prosecute; but in the case where he is not prosecuting he refuses to tell us what the advice was. There is not an hon. member of this house who does not know that if the minister had received advice not to prosecute, that would have been one of the first explanations we would have been given. So we can all draw the conclusion, which I am sure is the right one, that he received' a report recommending prosecution, and there is no other reason why he has not told us.
What I am pointing out right now is that a government which will follow that pattern in relation to a matter affecting the daily bread of the people of Canada will avail itself of the widest possible interpretation of every exception, such as those which have been just stated, if in its judgment it thinks some change should be made with respect to controls of this kind. I recall very well that last year the Minister of Finance, under whom this arbitrary authority is exercised, was ' 
unwilling to listen to any argument in regard to a change in procedure, but I suggest that he might still give consideration to a return to ordinary parliamentary procedure in this fifth year after the war and place before parliament a rent control bill which will contain in statutory form the assurance he has just given. If it is in fact the intention of the government that there shall be no change in the rental ceilings or in .the regulations as they now stand, the simplest way to remove from the minds of hon. members of this house the slightest suspicion that advantage may be taken of this exception would be to incorporate these provisions in a bill which when passed will become the law of the land and be binding upon the courts as well as the government.
As to whether those measures in themselves would be adequate and satisfactory, that would depend upon the way in which they were set out in statutory form. Surely, however, if it is the intention of the government to allow no change in the levels now established, if it is the intention of the government to prevent further rental increases, that can be simply stated in a bill which could be quickly drafted and presented to this house for consideration. What we are doing now is carrying forward wide, loose and arbitrary powers under which no Canadian affected by them knows what will be the situation. The minister says: Oh, you have my assurance, with qualifications. No matter how much we may be prepared to accept that assurance in its exact terms, we must remember that the government as a whole is in a position to decide, and that in certain cases the government as a whole in making decisions has availed itself of every latitude offered by the qualifications previously expressed.
I do not think the government would have any difficulty drafting such a bill. Every hon. member who has been in this house during the discussion of this important subject recalls the number of times the government has stated that it would be an easy thing for the provinces to deal with. I cannot believe this government feels that the provincial governments are so superior in intelligence that they could draft rent control bills which it would be beyond the competence of this government to present to this house. The very fact that they believe the provinces could deal with this question so readily is surely the best evidence that they believe it could be dealt with by a bill, because it must be remembered that the provincial governments could not deal with it by any arbitrary measure of this kind. They could deal with it only under a bill passed by the legislature.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, once again I urge upon the government the importance, not only from the point of view of security in the minds of those affected but also from the point of view of returning to sound parliamentary procedure, of not continuing this emergency power, but of the government presenting to this house immediately a clear, understandable and workable rent control bill.
Mr. J. W. Nose worthy (York South): Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us today, notwithstanding what we have just heard from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), I am sure will find a great deal of support in this house. The fact that it is sponsored by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will assure its passage here, regardless of the merit of the resolution itself. The circumstances leading up to the introduction of this resolution have created a great deal of public interest in the country.
There is today a great deal of public interest in both the resolution itself and the bill that will follow it. The bill that will follow this resolution will mark the culmination of the government's policy of wartime controls. All that is now left of those government controls is this little bit of rent control, a sort of relic of the former controls that were exercised under the Transitional Measures Act in the years since the war. One might question whether there is enough rent control left in Canada today to warrant all the trouble the government has gone to in order to establish its right to maintain that rent control. One might question whether this anaemic control will even outlive the next twelve-month period. As hon. members know, all the newer buildings which have been built since January 1, 1947, and all the newly-occupied houses and apartments since November 1, 1948, are already decontrolled and are unaffected by this resolution or the bill that will follow it.
Following on that was, of course, the government's permission for the increase of rents granted last fall which has already raised rents to just about all that the traffic can stand. There is not much particular merit in the statement made by the minister in his speech, giving the assurance that there would be no further changes in rents or no further increases during the coming year, since rents have already gone beyond the economic ability to pay of most people who rent homes.
' Even though this bill may not mean much to the people of Canada and even though its passage is assured by the large government majority back of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), I still think that something should be said with regard to the condition of rental housing at the present time. First of all, I
Transitional Measures Act should like to register again my protest, and that of the party to which I belong, against the government's callous indifference to and utter disregard of the problem which hundreds of thousands of tenants across Canada are called upon to meet as a result of the government's increased-rental order that was made last fall. The government have shown a flagrant disregard of the problems of these peftple who, in such large numbers, placed their confidence in them in June, 1949.
There is today an acute housing shortage. I am going to assume, Mr. Speaker, that one cannot very well talk about rent without talking about houses, since it is with the rental of houses that we are concerned in this resolution and the bill that will follow it. There is nothing that the government has done for housing during the last four or five years which can be considered as being particularly creditable. Today the housing shortage is more acute in Canada that it has ever been in our history. On January 1, 1946, the backlog of housing units needed at that time was given officially as 648,000. In 1946, 1947, and 1948 fewer houses were built each year than were required to meet the current need or to keep up with the current demand; 1949 is the first year in which the number of houses built exceeded the current need for that particular year. Whereas there was a backlog of 648,000 houses needed on January 1, 1946, there was on January 1, 1950, a backlog of 711,000. In other words there has been an increase of nearly 10 per cent since 1946. The general housing shortage is more acute today than it was four years ago. The backlog is greater than it was four years ago. The deficit is worse than it was four years ago. Overcrowding, particularly in our large cities, is worse than it was four years ago or at any other time in our history. Slums and substandard housing have scarcely been touched during those years. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in a brief submitted to the Massey commission last September, makes this statement:
The housing needs of the Canadian people have never been more critical than they are today.
If I may, I should like to review briefly the government's record in this respect because it is the government's failure over the years to meet the need that renders it necessary today for the minister to introduce the resolution that is now before us. The National Housing Act was first introduced in 1938. We were told then that its purpose was twofold: first, to provide home ownership through longterm federal loans at a low interest rate; and second, to provide homes for low income families through loans made to municipalities so that they might enter the field of building low-cost rental housing.

Transitional Measures Act
In the first three and a half years during which that National Housing Act was on our statute books, and at a time when there was a backlog of 500,000 houses needed, a sum total of 15,000 loans were made. Just think of it: 15,000 loans made to meet a backlog of housing units which at that time was estimated at 500,000. During those three and a* half years, because of the conditions which would attach to the lending of money to municipalities, not a single municipality in Canada took advantage of that part of the act which was designed to enable them to enter into an agreement with the federal government for the building of low-rental housing. In three and a half years not one single municipality felt itself able to avail itself of the benefits which were supposed to accrue under that act.
Then in 1944 the act was revised. Again the emphasis in the act was placed on the provision of homes built for sale, but particularly for the middle and upper class income families. For those in the lower income brackets, in 1944 the government sponsored an insurance company scheme for the building of low rental houses. Housing Enterprises Limited was established and was supposed to build 5,000 houses a year, which were to rent from $35 to $40. Housing Enterprises Limited was established in 1945. In 1947 Housing Enterprises collapsed. In the two years in which it had been in existence it had started, though it had not completed, not 5,000 houses a year, but 3,276 houses in the two years. It discovered that the rental of those houses was no longer $35 or $40 a month but anywhere up to $70. As an enterprise to meet the needs of the low-income group of people who want houses for rent, it is generally agreed that Housing Enterprises was a complete failure.
If we look at the National Housing Act during those years from the standpoint of providing homes for the low income group, we find it proved a failure. The only people who benefited under the National Housing Act were those in the middle and upper income groups, and the finance companies which provided the money.
In the field of slum clearance, the act provided a measure whereby the federal government would pay 50 per cent and the municipality 50 per cent of the cost. Something like $20 million was set aside for that purpose. Up to date only one project of slum clearance has been undertaken under that regulation, namely, the Regent Park project in Toronto. Another section of the National Housing Act provided for assistance in the building of farm houses, houses for rural people; and from the date on which the National Housing Act was first put on
TMr. Noseworthy.]
the statute books up until December, 1948, one lone farm house in all Canada had been built. Therefore I would say that for rural housing the act was not particularly successful. In the field of co-operative housing the act again just did not work.
Last fall, when speaking on the amendment to the National Housing Act, the minister himself admitted the act was ineffective in so far as co-operative housing was concerned. Today, even with the amendment to the act which we passed last fall, it still does not meet the need of those people who want low rent houses.
I have discovered that in Toronto no one earning less than $3,000 a year, which is approximately $60 a week,' can get a loan under the amended National Housing Act, to purchase a house. I hold in my hand a list of names and addresses, and the cost of the house, the monthly payment, and the income of the applicants. Application after application has been refused because the applicant himself was not in receipt of $3,000 a year. To apply for a loan in the city of Toronto the applicant must first get a statement from his employer showing how long and how regularly he has been employed. He must have a certified statement regarding what his annual income has been, and in every single case that I have examined where the income was less than $3,000 the applicant had been refused a loan. I have an instance of a husband and wife, both working, whose income together was well over $4,000. Yet the application was turned down because the man himself was earning only a few dollars below the $3,000 mark. Therefore for a purchaser to avail himself of a loan under the National Housing Act today he must earn at least $3,000 a year. That large group of wage earners, particularly in our large cities, who are not receiving $60 a week, or anything like it, are automatically excluded from the benefits of the act; and to date there is very little evidence that there are likely to be many, if any, projects undertaken in which the federal government and the provinces co-operate for the building of low rental houses.
A few days ago I asked a question when a notice appeared1 in the Toronto daily papers to the effect that the premier of Ontario had announced that his government was going to enter into an agreement with the federal government under the section of the National Housing Act which permits that co-operation in the building of low-cost rental housing. I inquired of the minister as to whether any agreement had been reached, or any negotiations carried on with the federal government, or whether

that was the accepted policy of the federal government. The answer in each and every instance was that there had been no agreement, that there had been no consultation, and that it could not be accepted as the present policy of the government to enter into that kind of agreement.
So that the situation in which we find ourselves today is that while there is a particularly acute shortage of general housing, that need is greatest of all in the field of rental housing. In 1941 we find that 58-9 per cent of all the houses occupied in Canada were rented. That is what we find from the census of that year. In the larger urban centres, with populations of 5,000 or more, the percentage of rented houses was then 65-8 per cent. At that time it would have required well over 100,000 houses to prevent overcrowding in those larger centres.
In other words there were about 1,250,000 rented houses in Canada at the time of that census, or between 4 million and 5 million Canadians in that year of 1941 who were living in rented accommodation. So that this question of rentals, the increase permitted last fall, and the whole matter of rental controls can be said, under present conditions, to affect about 5 million Canadians, or more. On the question of rentals the booklet called "Mortgage Lending in Canada", published in 1948 under the authority of the national housing administration, had this to say concerning the operations of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation:
The operations of the corporation indicate clearly that the housing need is much greater in the rental field than it is in the home ownership field. The supply of new rental housing, even including that built by the government, is only about 30 per cent of all residential construction. It is evident that many purchasers of new houses would have preferred to rent rather than purchase.
On the question of overcrowding, I think there is no one who will gainsay the remark that the housing emergency today is most acute for the poorest section of the nation, and that overcrowding is worse among the low-income group.
In 1941 we find, according to the census figures for that year, that 29 per cent of the entire population was living in overcrowded conditions. With the increased urbanization that has taken place since that time, and with the increased shortage of housing, that percentage would be much higher today than it was at that time. Even then, of those in the income bracket of $1,500 or less, there were at that time 40 per cent living in overcrowded conditions.
That was the condition in 1941, and certainly it is much worse today. The ordinary worker in these days just cannot buy any of
Transitional Measures Act the houses being built-certainly none of the houses built from loans made by the national housing administration. Last year the average cost of a dwelling unit, built with the assistance of loans from the housing administration, was $8,056. The average in cities is much higher than that. For instance, in Toronto it is impossible to buy even a one-storey bungalow of three and a half rooms- including the bathroom-for $8,000. Today accommodation of that kind ranges anywhere from $9,000 to $10,000.
On the assumption that the purchaser should not spend more than 20 per cent of his income on housing accommodation, there are only two or three groups of industrial workers who could possibly buy any of the houses being built. On that basis the only people who could buy even the very cheapest houses built with the aid of national housing administration loans are some who are working in the western coal-mining industry, the metal-mining industry, the steam railways and the pulp and paper industry.
Industrial workers in all of the nine leading industrial groups in Canada, including those engaged in manufacturing, iron and steel production, the automobile industry and building construction, receive incomes which, on the basis set forth by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, would preclude any of them from buying even the cheapest houses built.
Therefore there is today a great need for housing accommodation among people in that class. Of the 711,000 houses needed in Canada today I believe I would be correct in saying that by far the greater percentage of them are needed by those in income brackets which do not permit their buying at current building costs.
The bill that will follow this resolution will bring relief to that section of our people who are still living in rented houses that have not been decontrolled. As I have pointed out, large numbers of rented houses in this country have become decontrolled at various stages, but I understand that there is a fairly large section that will be affected by the bill to follow this resolution. I am quite sure that many hundreds of thousands of Canadians will breathe a sigh of relief when they read the minister's statement of this afternoon that there will be no further increases in their rents until April, 1951.
However good this legislation may be, it does not go far enough toward dealing with the root of the rental problem. Unless the federal government takes the initiative of entering into negotiations with the provincial governments whereby projects may be undertaken to provide low rental housing for the

Transitional Measures Act masses of our people whose income is less than $3,000 per year we shall still have reached no solution to our housing problem. It is that that I urge upon the government during this debate.

Mr. Speaker, in rising for the first time this session I deem it necessary to thank two great men in Canada for the opportunity of representing the constituency of Rosedale in this house. It is well known to hon. members that this riding returned to the Liberal party after being represented by members of the opposition for some fifty years. I have to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the excellent leadership which he and other members of the government gave during the election campaign of June, 1949. I have also to thank the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) for the manner in which he conducted his campaign and the attitudes he adopted at that time. As a result of these attitudes by way of a secondary reason, I am here today. I noticed a display of these campaign attitudes here today in this debate.
I note that in this debate as in others the attitude of the opposition seems to be, "We in the opposition agree with what the government is doing, but we think the government is doing it in the wrong way." The people of Rosedale objected to that general attitude on the part of the leader of the opposition and I think that was a factor in their turning to the Liberal party after many years of absence therefrom.
I think rent control has the approval of all hon. members in so far as the principle is concerned. Even as a newcomer to this house I recognized the necessity of bringing to the government's attention the need for the continuance of rent control, particularly within the Toronto area. As early as October 20, 1949, I drew this to the attention of the government, in a public way. I am pleased to see the continuance of rent control by this legislation now before us.
Last fall I received certain representations, many of a serious nature, from groups and individuals in my constituency objecting to the increases in rents which were permissibly made under the regulations. As a matter of duty I brought those to the attention of the government, but the permissive increases were put through notwithstanding. The inability to please all areas and groups arises from the administration of this measure at the national rather than the provincial level. It may be that greater satisfaction would have been achieved in the Toronto area if the provincial government had taken over rent control in the fall of last year when it was

offered to them by the federal government. However, there seems to be apathy on the part of the provincial government in this connection and if the present housing emergency does not subside it may be that the provincial government will have an opportunity after thirteen months have passed of doing what perhaps they should have done in the fall of last year.
Positive steps have been taken by the federal government to solve the housing shortage. It is notable that during the last general election the housing shortage in the Toronto area was a critical issue, if I may put it that way, raised by the opposition parties and answered by the government candidates. The jury of public opinion in Toronto during the last federal election gave its decision in a definite manner. The result was most emphatic because today there are several Liberal members in this house which indicates the confidence of the people of Toronto in the government of the day.
Prompt action was taken at the last session in connection with housing. A total of $300 million was allotted under the amendments to the National Housing Act. It is only fair to say that that allotment of money has enabled the government of Ontario to go on with low-cost rental housing projects in the London and other areas, all of which will become a reality in the near future. I have not a copy of the verbatim report of the debates in the legislature of Ontario, but it is apparent from the press reports that the premier of Ontario intends to take advantage of the provisions of the National Housing Act and proceed with projects which will make available homes with a down payment in the neighbourhood of $500. This will be the result of co-operation between the dominion and the province of Ontario.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) seemed to belittle the efforts of the government in connection with large scale land clearances and the low-cost subsidized housing that would result therefrom. In the lower part of Rosedale riding is located the Regent Park housing development which is an example of what can result from co-operation between three levels of government, dominion, provincial and municipal. I am frank to state that the plausible, good-natured and well respected Tory mayor of the wartime period, Robert Saunders, came to Ottawa towards the end of the war and was received gladly by the minister then in charge of the National Housing Act, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). There arose out of their cordial conversations the Regent Park scheme.

I should like to give you a few details to show what has been done in this case where there was good will on all sides. The Regent Park project consists of a housing development within six square city blocks in the lower part of Rosedale riding. The land was expropriated by the city, and there are to be constructed thereon apartments on a low-cost-rental subsidized basis. The share of the dominion government is put forward for clearance of the land and the substandard houses are removed on a basis of 50 per cent payable by the dominion government and 50 per cent by the municipality. Under the proposed scheme the share contributed by the federal government is $1,150,000. This constitutes a sum which, if capitalized over the fifty year "lifetime" period of the scheme, at three per cent represents a contribution on the part of the federal government of $33,000 per year.
The citizens of Rosedale constituency in Toronto can consider that during the lifetime of the scheme the federal government is in effect contributing towards low cost rental housing in the area the sum of $33,000 per year. As I understand it, the government of the province of Ontario has to date matched the contributions of the federal government dollar for dollar. Ownership of the project is in the name of the city and it contributes the balance of the cost of construction. You may ask, what of the rents under this low-cost housing scheme? I have to tell you that the rents are based on an equitable rule, namely, "one week's pay of the family income for one month's rent." There are sixty-five apartment units erected to date and the average rent is $52 per month. It is noteworthy that the plan of rent is such that if the family income falls through unemployment, then the rent comes down, and presumably if their income rises then the rent goes up. This is a most equitable method of establishing subsidized low cost rental housing in the area.
I have been in these apartments and they are of the finest construction. It is noteworthy that citizens from outside the six square blocks telephone me and ask how they may procure an apartment in the Regent Park development scheme. So far one-third of the apartments planned have been the subject of a contract, and further action is being taken. In the end there will be 1,056 apartments. A group of 3,000 people are housed in the area now but when the project is completed there will be 4,000 there. Accommodation will be provided for 1,000 more people, and I know it is welcomed by the people of my constituency. It is not unfair to suggest that this notable effort in the field of housing was made by the federal government for the
Transitional Measures Act constituency despite the fact that, at the time it was instituted, the constituency was represented by a former member of the opposition.
I should like to point out to the minister before I take my seat that the housing problem in my constituency is not confined to the southern area only. There is a residential section of some thirty-five to forty years' standing north of Bloor street which is known to residents of Toronto as Rosedale proper. The need for housing in Toronto during the emergency of the war was great, and in that area there were many large homes containing up to twenty or thirty rooms each. Automatically they became establishments for the housing of certain troops and other people on wartime duties. Then the guest home movement increased in the area, and it was found necessary as a war measure to pass order No. 200 of the wartime prices and trade board which in effect superseded the residential bylaws of the city. It is one of the orders which will be renewed under this statute which we are discussing today. In the area there are not less than 200 to 300 guest homes housing upwards of 3,000 people who can be said to be for the most part white collar office workers. Order No. 200 of the wartime prices and trade board in effect legalizes the living conditions of the 3,000 people living in these guest homes. When the order is lifted, or the time comes when the government does not have the power to keep order No. 200 in effect, there are the bylaws of the city which prevent the existence of guest homes on a legal basis and the occupancy thereof by the tenants. It is recognized by the city that time marches on, and that perhaps the character of the area has changed. It is recognized that something should be done to protect the proprietary investment of the people who commenced operation of these homes during wartime, and also to protect the housing accommodation of the guests living in these homes.
I recognize that this is primarily a municipal matter. Nevertheless I think that the experience of the wartime rental administration of the government as it is recorded might be given to the municipal authorities for their guidance and benefit when they come to consider what provisions it may be necessary to change in the municipal residential bylaws. I say to the minister that if the city so desires it-and I think they would be glad to have it-he should make available to them the recorded information available in the rental administration of the wartime prices and trade board. I would also ask him to make available the services of his law officers when and if it becomes necessary. I think

Transitional Measures Act that is the least we can do because this problem will arise for solution on the municipal level sooner or later.
I conclude with this thought. Legislation having to do with rents and housing comes within the category of "must" legislation. It is a fact that until this government was returned at the last election the operation of this legislation was hampered, and that our housing legislation could be found just around the corner of interprovincial disunity. I commend the premier of Ontario for his spirit of co-operation, and in particular for his attitude toward the amalgamation of the city of Toronto and the outlying municipalities in that area. The mandate given candidates in the federal election was clear. National unity is the order of the day; and I believe that at the bar of interprovincial public opinion we are most fortunate in having the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his colleagues in the cabinet, because they are without peers in this matter of national and interprovincial unity. I look forward to great things in future from our housing legislation and its administrative bodies.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I followed with some interest the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry) and the obvious satisfaction he took from the fact that seven Liberal members were returned from Toronto ridings at the last general election. In the view of the hon. member that seems to be quite sufficient to permit him to sit back now with complete complacency and behold with satisfaction the present state of affairs. If I am not mistaken, among the plethora of promises made by Liberal candidates in Toronto, which they hoped would help them to be elected, one made by the hon. member for Rosedale was that if he were elected he would see the housing problem solved, to use his own words, "before the snow flies".

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I deny that, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I accept the hon. member's statement, of course. I did not bring the file here with me, and I said I thought it was the hon. member who had made that statement. He denies it, and I do not intend to question his denial; but I am going to have a look at some newspaper files on the subject. At any rate that statement was made by one of those candidates, whose election no doubt was thereby helped.
If hon. members can contemplate housing conditions in Toronto and elsewhere with satisfaction, I am afraid they either do not know or are not concerned about the conditions under which many people are living. If housing conditions are so satisfactory it is


probably unnecessary for hon. members to engage in the discussion of any legislative needs; but I was interested in what the hon. member had to say about the Regent Park development. The suggestion or inference the hon. member invited us to draw from his statement was that this Regent Park development was made possible only through assistance given by the federal government. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of some personal connection with the planning of that development in the first place, when I was a member of the Toronto city council, that the contribution by the federal authority to that housing undertaking was very small indeed. That is the one instance, as far as I am aware, in which a slum clearance program has been undertaken in Canada. It was a matter of satisfaction to us that when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) went to Toronto last year and saw it, he acclaimed it as an eye-opener. From that many of us hoped the government would be prepared to make some show of generosity in helping to bring about the elimination of such slum conditions that exist in many of the urban centres of Canada.
What actually happened? I have mentioned that in this case the contribution of the federal authority was very small. Actually it amounted to only one-half the cost of land acquisition under section 12 of the housing act. After the Prime Minister's visit and the way he lauded the development, which was made possible largely by the enterprise of those concerned in the municipal government in Toronto, one might have expected that this sort of enterprise would be encouraged elsewhere. When the amendments to the housing act were brought down here last fall, however, we found that not one cent more was provided for reconstruction projects of that kind than was available previously. We still are limited to section 12 of the housing act, under which the federal authority contributes only one-half the cost of land assembly; and the amendments of 1949 do not help at all in the case of reconstruction projects.
I brought this to the attention of the house when we were in committee of the whole on those amendments. At that time I pleaded with the minister to extend the provisions, or to put upon the amendments an interpretation which would make those provisions available to assist in reconstruction projects. The minister had this to say, at page 2447 of Hansard for November 29, 1949:
I think it is clear, Mr. Chairman, that where there is a section already in the act, namely section 12, providing for the redevelopment of land, it is not intended that this section should apply.

That was the new section contained in the amendments. That is the situation; and if the hon. member for Rosedale sees merit in the Regent Park development would you not have thought he would welcome the opportunity to rise, as I think I invited him and all Toronto Liberal members to do on the occasion to which I just referred, when these amendments were under discussion on November 29 last, and give some support to my request that the amendments be extended to include redevelopment projects? But the voice of the hon. member, along with the voices of the other Liberal members elected from Toronto, was silent. They did not have a word to say in support of the suggestion that assistance should be given to slum clearance by way of more generous contributions on the part of the federal authority to reconstruction projects.
I propose to speak very briefly on the resolution before us today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I can be longer if my hon. friend continues to encourage me.
I believe the statement my leader made today has put our position on this matter so clearly that no elaboration is required. I wish, therefore, to dwell on only two, or at the most three, points.
My leader called for a proper bill to put into correct legislative form the statutory enactments necessary to continue rent control, and urged that this subject, which is of such great importance, should not be left in the clumsy form in which the government asks that it be continued. The minister has stated that the powers conferred by the bill to be founded on this resolution are confined to price and rent control. He said all the other powers provided by the bill had disappeared except those concerning price and rent control, and indicated that it is not the intention of the government to make any changes in general in the present scheme.
Sir, if the bill is to have as confined an effect as the minister suggests, then the case for a proper rent control bill is stronger than it has ever been before. A year ago when this measure was under debate, the government indicated that there were twelve orders in council whose effect was to be continued by the bill. The minister has not given to the house today the particular orders that are to be continued by the bill. I take it that there are at most probably only two or three; probably they are P.C. 8528, P.C. 9029 and P.C. 5518. Those are the general orders in council which are to be continued, as I understand his statement, although on this point we shall ask for more information when we are
Transitional Measures Act in committee on the resolution. But, sir, the fact that, according to the minister's statement, the scope of these controls is to be confined now to rent control emphasizes, to a degree not hitherto present, the fact that it is quite unnecessary now to carry on this remaining hodgepodge of orders in council which will be continued if the measure before the house remains in its present form.
On the other aspect of the minister's statement I have one or two observations to make. My leader has already commented upon the statement of the minister, who said that it is not the intention of the government to interfere with the present rent ceilings or the present freezing regulations, except in certain cases. If the government's intention is so simple, sir, simple legislation now would suffice for the purpose without carrying on this hodgepodge of orders in council and the sweeping powers that are reposed in the government under the Transitional Measures Act.
What is the effect of a statement made by the government? We in the official opposition had some complaint to make in times past about the weight attached by the government to statements emanating from the government. What are these statements of intention? Are they binding assurances? If they are binding assurances, there should be no hesitation on the part of the government in writing them into the text of legislation. But the government does not seem to be anxious to see those statements of intention written into legislative form.
Let me give one or two illustrations of the weight attached by the government itself to statements of the kind that it has made in the house; and in this connection I ask hon. members to bear in mind the situation in which great numbers of people in this country found themselves at the beginning of last November when, without any warning whatsoever, without any reference to this house, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) simply announced sweeping changes in the rent ceilings, changes which affected hundreds of thousands of people whose protests, incidentally, were completely unavailing because parliament had no power to interfere.
The legislation was there, and the government exercised the power by order in council. As long as parliament is going to repose in this government powers by order in council to interfere with the contractual relationships between landlords and tenants on the scale on which those relationships were interfered with by those orders in council early last November, sir, the parliament of Canada will be completely by-passed. Parliament will not be consulted. Parliament will even have to sit by while the government

Transitional Measures Act takes measures that will interfere with the rights of the people and affect those rights far more than anything that will be done by direot action on the.part of this parliament. That, sir, is a fundamentally wrong method; and I submit that it is high time parliament made up its mind that it will not any longer countenance such things. Where measures are required, as in this case they are, in respect of rent control, this parliament should take that responsibility; and parliament should reserve to itself, and to itself alone, the right to change, modify or terminate those measures. It should not be left to the whim of the government.
The minister invites us to accept, in lieu of or as a substitute for proper legislation, in a matter of high importance to the people of Canada, statements of intention on the part of the government. Let us consider the history of some such statements in the past. Sir, you and I well remember the statement made in this house in 1946, found at page 2547 of Hansard of that year, in which the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, in relation to a measure then before the house with regard to foreign exchange control, said:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
That certainly was a clear statement on the part of the government. What was the result? When it suited the government in November, 1947, to use powers in defiance of that assurance given to the house, powers which they purported to find in the very measure which was then under comment by Mr. Ilsley, they exercised those powers and, if you please, did it by radio decree without the slightest consultation of parliament. In a matter of such paramount importance to hundreds of thousands of Canadians, is it to be assumed by this house that the statement made by the Minister of Finance today will be given any higher regard or effect by the government when it suits their purposes at some future time to qualify it or to disregard it entirely, or that they will pay any more attention to it than was paid by the same government to this strong statement made by Mr. Ilsley in 1946?
You will not have forgotten, sir-and 1 am sure the house will not have forgotten- that when the present Minister of Finance was pressed in the house about that statement made by his predecessor in the same portfolio, an assurance that he himself was simply throwing overboard and was in effect completely repudiating, his answer was that it was only a statement that Mr. Ilsley made; he said that it was not a binding undertaking given to the house, but only a statement.


In the face of that experience, the same minister today asks us? to accept, as a substitute for proper legislation, a statement on his part of the intention of the government in relation to circumstances as they appear to him to exist now. I say to you, sir, that this parliament cannot accept that statement made by the minister today as any substitute for proper legislation.
Then, sir, the Minister of Finance is not alone in the estimate that he places upon statements or assurances emanating from the government. I well recall that in this house a year ago, when a statement was made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in which he announced that it was the policy of the government to ask the house to approve a loan of $4 million to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the development of television in Canada, I rose and asked him this question, as reported at page 2837 of Hansard:
Will the radio committee have an opportunity of reviewing this policy and reporting to the house before the house Is called upon to approve the loan of $4 million.
The answer of the minister was:	"The
answer is definitely yes." You will find that recorded in Hansard. That was a direct and categorical statement, one would have thought. If statements by the government are treated seriously by the government, one could not have asked for a more categorical statement than that one. But what happened to that statement? In December of last year it suited the purposes of the government to ignore that promise completely, to repudiate it, and to push through this house the same loan without the radio committee having been appointed or ever having had the opportunity to make the study which it had been promised that the committee should make before the government would ask the house to approve this loan of $4 million to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for that purpose.
Now, sir, there are other instances. I think those two are sufficient to indicate the estimate which the government puts upon its own statements to the house. And if the house or the country, in the face of the repudiation of those statements by the government when it suited their purpose, chooses to attach to the statement made by the Minister of Finance today some efficacy in substitution for proper legislation, then, sir, the responsibility will rest on those who are prepared to put in jeopardy the rights of Canadians by hundreds of thousands.
I say to you, sir, that parliament in a matter so important, must not continue the hodgepodge of sweeping arbitrary powers contained in this act. It dare not ignore its responsibility to enact clear legislation that

will provide protection to those whose rights will be thereby affected, and who are entitled to know what their rights and liabilities are. If this parliament ignores that duty and chooses to accept ministerial statements which in the past have been treated so lightly by the government, then, sir, the majority in this house must accept the responsibility.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the people of my province of Manitoba, and of my city of Winnipeg in particular, have a double-barrelled grievance in connection with this whole matter of rent control. They have been misled twice within the past year. It is not yet a year since the federal election campaign was under way, when security for our people in every form was a Liberal propaganda item, when our people were led to believe that by returning Liberals to power they could get all of the security, all of the protection that was in the C.C.F. program.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I am interested in the laughter that I am hearing from the Liberals on the other side of the house. It turns out now that in their opinion it was quite a joke that was played on our people. There was no notion in the minds of the people of Winnipeg, or the people of Manitoba, last June, that within four or five months after a sweeping Liberal victory action would be taken such as that on November 3, of permitting a further drastic increase in rent, which this legislation will not correct, since it merely keeps in effect for another year the ceilings established at that time.
Despite the fact that our people were misled in that way last June, they went through the same experience again in Winnipeg and in Manitoba last November. It was on November 3 that the Minister of Finance rose in his place in this house and announced the increases that were to become effective as at December 15. A provincial election was under way in Manitoba at that very time. Candidates of all parties, especially in the city of Winnipeg, realized what a burning issue it was, and they literally tumbled over each other trying to get in there first. Candidates of all parties promised that they would do something about it. The promises varied from one offer to another. Some of them were going to take over rent controls in the province right away. Others were going to press the federal government to retain -the ceilings where they had been, and others of course would just have the matter looked into. But that promise to do something about rent control was made, as I say, by both Liberals and Conservatives in the coalition, and by the members of all parties

I hope the people of Manitoba realize they are now being handed the same kind of half assurances that they were given by the Liberals prior to the 27th of June. Oh, no. I continue with the quotation I was giving:
Once the 10th of November is past, any thought that the Manitoba government would take over rent control in that province is just as far down the drain as is the promise of the federal government that they would protect the health and the living standards of the Canadian people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to support what I said a moment ago about that quotation being from an expert, and to make it clear that I was not just patting myself on the back, but that what I said was an accurate forecast of what would happen, I call the attention of the house to the issue of the Winnipeg Free Press dated March 22, just two days ago, the main story of which relates to a debate in the Manitoba legislature on the question of rent control. The official opposition in the legislature, which is the C.C.F., presented to the Manitoba house a motion condemning the provincial government for not taking over rent control and operating it on a provincial basis. What happened? The government moved an amendment to that motion expressing its complete confidence in federal rent control, thus sidetracking the real issue before that house; and a good many of the members who were candidates in the election and had promised that they would see to it that rent control was taken over voted for the government's amendment and thus defeated the proposal which called upon the provincial government to take over rent control as the Minister of Finance is urging them to do. Therefore the people of Manitoba find that they have been fooled twice, first on the 27th of June and again on the 10th of November, so far as rent control is concerned. They were led to believe on both

Transitional Measures Act occasions that by voting Liberal their rental situation would be protected. They now find that these promises have again gone down the drain, just as I indicated in my remarks on November 8 of last year.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, no one can vote against this measure. There is not much to it, but anything less would be unthinkable. All this measure does is to continue in effect the high ceiling on rents that is now in effect. It does not give to the people of the country any relief from high rents. It does not roll them back to what they were last December.
I could point out, as the minister said, that one province, facing up to its responsibility, accepted the minister's offer and agreed to take over rent control starting on April 1. That is the province of Saskatchewan. The result is that most rents in that province are still at the level which was in effect last December.
The people of Manitoba wanted something similar done in their province, whether by the federal government or by the provincial government. But they find that, despite the credence they have given to Liberal promises and Liberal assurances, they are not going to get it either way. The government in the provincial legislature moves an amendment expressing confidence in the federal administration of rent controls, and that meaningless motion carries. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) rises in the house and reads from a supreme court judgment, of which he approves, saying that this whole business is really a provincial matter, and makes it very clear that within thirteen months it will be thrown back to the. provinces, in its entirety. What a hope!
It so happens that the constituency I represent has in it a large number of tenants who are affected by rent control. I can tell the minister and the house that during the two days I was home last November, when this issue was being fought out in the provincial election campaign, the protests over what was taking place were literally legion. Since then, next to the interest people have shown in the removal of the means test from old age pensions, this has been the question which has been the greatest concern of the people I represent.
I feel strongly about this. I feel that ever since the war the whole attitude toward rent control on the part of the government has been one of callous indifference to what has been happening to the Canadian people, particularly to workers who are tenants, who have had their rents raised time and again, making it extremely difficult for them to get along. Old age pensioners and others on


small fixed incomes have had it very hard, too.
I agree with the position taken today by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) when he states that this matter ought to have been put in proper legislative form long ago. It seems to me that one of the things this parliament must somehow put a stop to is the way in which the government constantly arrogates power to itself which it can exercise without any reference whatever to parliament. We should have matters like this in statutory form so that we can approve or disapprove of them at the time they are being enacted, and so that we will know where we stand.
This method of legislating has given the government far too much power. The minister may say it has given them power at times to impose controls, which power they exercised during the war. But the only way they have exercised it since the war has been to continue to permit these increases.
I am not the only one in the house who is aware of the misery and suffering this brings to our people. Liberal members are aware of it, too. Indeed, they were very much aware of it last November, at the time the minister made his announcement; and my guess is that they have been getting just as many letters in the last few months as I have about the increases that have been taking place.
So we are in this position, that we will vote for the measure before the house because it will keep in effect what little control now obtains. But it is a pretty sad story, this whole business, the way this question of rent control has been handled. It has not been rent control at all; it has been rent decontrol, with many anomalies which have created all sorts of difficulties with complete unfairness to the people of this country as a whole.
There is something further I should like to say about this matter. Frankly, I do not like to be a suspicious person. I do not like questioning assurances given to me, particularly when they are given across the floor of the house.	.
