speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There is something to the humorous interjection just made by the hon. member for Souris. I have been here long enough now to become sceptical of assurances. Far too often positive assurances given to us have not been kept. Today we have it again. We are given an assurance the keeping of which need not worry us too much, for the assurance is that a ceiling which is just about up to the sky will not be raised any higher during the next thirteen months.

However, this raises the whole question of parliament's being asked to satisfy itself with ministerial assurance rather than with clear-cut legislation put on the statute books.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed to a couple of cases, and I shall point to several more, where ministerial assurances have been broken. One of them relates to a statute placed on the statute books, but one which contained an escape clause-just as there is an escape phrase in the assurance given by the minister today. And when it suited the government it used that escape clause, not just in a few instances of emergency, but used it 100 per cent.
The case I have in mind relates to the government's policy with regard to civil aviation. Hon. members here in the parliament before last will remember the present Minister of Trade and Commerce laying it down as firm government policy that within a year after the end of the war in Europe all railway companies were to be compelled to divest themselves of the ownership of any air lines. Not only was it laid down as policy in speeches delivered by the minister and in assurances given to the house-a policy which, by the way, was opposed bitterly by the official opposition; so that it cannot be said that it was non-contentious-but it was written into a statute.
I have here the act in question, to be found in the statutes for 1944-45, chapter 28 of which is an act to amend the Aeronautics Act. Section 12 (2) of that act states:
No such licence shall be issued in respect of a commercial air service, owned, leased, controlled or operated by any person who is engaged in the transport of goods or passengers for hire or reward by means other than aircraft unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such licence be issued.
And then turning to section 14, which is lengthy, we find it states-and I summarize- that every licence then in effect was to expire within one year after the end of the war in Europe.
So there, in statutory form, it was laid down that all of these companies, such as the air lines owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway, were to be separated from ownership by railway companies, and no further licences to railway companies to operate air lines were to be granted.
Time went on. We reached a point one year after the end of the war in Europe. Then we got into the second year, at which time I began asking questions about it. What did we find? We found that, first of all, the government by a minute of council-a quite improper procedure-decided that that one year was to be treated as two years- in violation of the act-and then they
Transitional Measures Act further got around the act by letting all licences to aviation companies then in existence expire-every one of them. Then they .reissued the whole lot under the terms of that emergency clause in section 12(2).
How do hon. members expect us to accept with complete assurance the statement made today by the minister, with an escape phrase in his statement, when we have had experiences such as the one I have described?
Then I think of some other assurances we have been given. During the session of 1948 I was a bit of a bother to the government over the question of its aviation policy in the Pacific. I had heard rumours that it was going to change its clearly-stated policy, namely that T.C.A. was to fly the Pacific. So I asked question after question, in one form or another, and was given the assurance that there was no change in that item of clearly-stated government policy. The session ended, and we went home. Within a week or so an announcement was made of a change in government policy, to the effect that flying the Pacific for Canada was being turned over to Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
I remind hon, members of what happened in August 1946 when there was before the house a motion calling upon the government to reconsider its announced intention of taking the second subsidy off milk. An amendment to a motion to go into supply was carried by the house. By a majority vote the house called upon the government to reconsider that matter. We asked the government what it would do about it, and were assured that the matter would be reconsidered. Then in a few days parliament was prorogued. A couple of weeks later the result of that reconsideration was that the subsidy was taken off, contrary to the expressed wish of parliament, and the price of milk went up.
Another instance that comes to my mind occurred on June 30, 1948. At that session we had had quite a bit of discussion about government annuities. By order in council the government had changed the basic interest rate upon which the annuities are based. As a result of protests from all sections of the house the promise was finally made by the government through the Minister of ' Labour (Mr. Mitchell) on June 30, 1948, that a special committee would be set up at the next session to go into the whole matter. When I asked at the next session, and the next, when that committee was going to be set up I was unable to get a satisfactory answer from the minister. The plain fact of the matter is that the promise was ignored; another assurance was broken.

Transitional Measures Act
A few days ago the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) read from Hansard of April, 1945, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) introduced t his white paper on post-war employment projects. My colleague read the specific statement that was made as to committees that would be set up, the money that would be voted, the way in which the government would implement that clear-cut assurance. Now the whole business has gone by the board.
When we were arguing last fall with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) about the McGregor report the minister assured us- although I certainly did not accept the assurance-that the report which he had received the previous December was really not in final form until October, 1949. In other words, the minister then-this was not his first answer; it was one of his subsequent answers-assured us across the floor of this house that he had kept the law, that he had tabled the report within fifteen days of its being in his hands in final form.
However, on March 22, just a couple of days ago, the same Minister of Justice in answer to some questions put on the order paper by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) let slip this bit of information, namely, that that report was referred on July 11, 1949, to J. J. Kelly, K.C., of Winnipeg for a legal opinion as to whether or not prosecution of the millers should be gone ahead with. It so happened that Mr. Kelly was subsequently appointed to the Court of King's Bench-that would be on the recommendation of the same Minister of Justice-and the matter was referred to another lawyer, T. N. Phelan, K.C., of Toronto, on September 20, 1949.
There it is in black and white that the report was in complete form so that the government could refer it to counsel for an opinion as to whether or not to go ahead and prosecute, and yet last fall the minister got up in this house and gave us his assurance that he was keeping the law when he knew as well as the rest of us did that he was not.
It is instances of that sort, and we are having far too many in this parliament, which make me sceptical about the statement the minister made today. The only reason that I can see for one counting on today's assurance being kept is its substance. The ceiling is now so high that the government could hardly push it any higher. If the ceiling were lower I am afraid the assurance would be in the same category as some of those we have had before.
We will have to support this measure to keep in effect for another thirteen months


such federal rent control as we have, but I felt that I should take the time to register once again the protests of the people I represent against the way in which they have been fooled in connection with rent control. I felt also that I should take time to document the contention which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and others have put forward as to the value of government promises. The government must get away from these ministerial assurances and get down to more clear-cut statements, which should be put down in black and white-in proper legislative form- so we will know where we stand.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to hold up this measure and I shall speak for only a few minutes, but there are a few things I should like to say. In fact what is before the house at this time is nothing. There has not been any rent control for some considerable time. All the minister proposes to do is to extend something that has not existed for quite a long time.
I look upon this matter of retaining rent control very seriously because it has been a long-drawn-out controversy in this country. It is in connection with this measure that I ran into the greatest amount of apprehension in all sections of the constituency that I have the privilege to represent and in all parts of the country that I was able to visit after the election was over. When it became apparent that the federal government were desirous of getting out of rent control various bodies like the Canadian Legion and the Canadian Congress of Labour were sufficiently interested to take the matter to the courts in order to test its validity. Those two bodies represent a large section of the people of Canada that requires either housing or the control of what housing there is.

speechtext:
It is significant to consider the petition which is now before the other place from the company which is seeking this incorporation here tonight, where one finds that they have been applying for incorporation in order to build a pipe line on a route lying through the United States. The route has been fully described as that route which leads just across the southeast corner of our province; then it proceeds through the states of Idaho and Washington to the Pacific coast, where it splits into two branches, one going south to Oregon and the other going back up north to Vancouver.
I should like hon. members who disagree with our position to consider carefully the merits of their suggestion that we should allow this bill to go through, since, it is said,


all that is sought here is the incorporation of a company, and that we should let the Alberta government decide on the route of the line, or let the board of transport commissioners decide it. Mr. Speaker, I am not speaking as a legal or constitutional expert, although I have given some study to the matter, but I believe that a very good case could be made out for the contention that neither the Alberta government nor the board of transport commissioners has any legal or constitutional authority to control the export of gas from Canada. The Alberta board is concerned primarily with assuring that sufficient supplies of gas are in that province to meet the foreseeable requirements of Alberta over the next fifty years. Once they have satisfied themselves on that score, they will consider granting licences to export gas; but I submit that if the Alberta board were to refuse to license the export of gas merely on the ground that the proposed line crosses the international border, their decision would be declared ultra vires, because that would be an interference with interprovincial and export trade. I submit they will have no authority to refuse to license on those grounds. In the same way, if hon. members will consider carefully the main oil and gas Pipe Lines Act under which the companies must apply to the board of transport commissioners for authorization, they will find in that act that the question of whether the line goes to the United States is not a consideration to be taken into account by the board in granting or refusing their application. You will not find any authority for the board to take into consideration the question whether or not the line has to be built into the United States. There is no authority, expressed or implied, for the board to refuse their authority merely because the company propose to build their line across the border. I submit that, in the same way, it would be ultra vires the board of transport commissioners to refuse to grant their authority to build a line merely . because it is proposed to send it through the United States.
Indeed I would presume this matter has been given some consideration by those who are now applying for incorporation, because we find they have laid down the route they propose to build, and it shows clearly that for the greater part of its length it is to be through the United States. If they thought that the board could refuse or might refuse their application because of that fact they would not have included it in their petition. Therefore I say the only way we can be certain that the policy of building the line through Canada is followed is to insist upon the assurance being given by the sponsors of the bill before we pass it. If it is the desire

to cut short this debate, and if it is desired by hon. members who say that they believe in the policy of Canada first, if it is desired to ensure that we shall have the line through Canada, then I suggest that the way to do it, and the way to cut short this debate, would be to amend the main Pipe Lines Act to provide that the board shall not grant authority unless the line is built through Canada. If that were done, then certainly I would cease my opposition to the bill, and I believe I can safely say that other hon. members who have been opposing it would cease their opposition; because then we would find that the line would be built through Canada, and we would be content to grant incorporation to as many companies as wish to build the line through Canada first.
However, until that assurance is given, or until the Pipe Lines Act is amended so that we may have the line built through Canada serving Canadian cities, and serving this country, with the benefits of the enormous cost of construction and the employment which will come to Canada-I say until that is done we must continue to oppose the incorporation of these companies because, in our view, it would be a great disservice to Canada and a negation of the principle that we must now build up our economy to provide opportunities for employment and expansion here at home.
On that basis I take my stand squarely in opposition to the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the purpose of the bill now before the house is to incorporate a certain number of people under the name Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
These persons are seeking permission to build and operate pipe lines for carrying gas and oil from - sources in Alberta to certain points both within and outside of Canada.
The bill, however, carefully avoids any description of the route along which the promoters intend to build their pipe line. No map is attached, as is usual when railway companies seek incorporation.
The matter before the house has been discussed during at least two sessions. I do not think there is any precedent on record of such a lengthy discussion on a private bill.
So far more than thirty members have spoken for or against this measure. Two party chieftains, the leader of the opposition
Prairie Transmission Lines (Mr. Drew) and the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) have taken part in the debate and voiced strong opposition to the bill.
At first, representatives of the provinces concerned, Alberta and British Columbia, were the only ones to show their interest in the matter by taking part in the debate, that has been rather bitter at times. But today, members from all parts of Canada, even from Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, have spoken on the bill, an indication of the importance of this measure. It also goes to show that the more we talk about it in the house, the more significant it becomes.
We must conclude, from what we read in the newspapers that it is a most vital question. We surely have grounds to wonder why it is so important and why it receives so much attention in the house.	[DOT]
In my opinion, members of the opposition took part in this debate because it dealt with the nation's natural resources and because it is in line with the "Canada first" policy, always practised by my party.
A nation's natural resources are its most valuable assets. It is the duty of every Canadian, whatever his home province and whatever the issue at stake, to see to the conservation of our country's natural resources and to their development in the best interest of our people.
If such is the duty of every citizen, I believe that the government, on whom rests so many responsibilities, has the dual obligation of considering the matter and making sure that the interests of our people as a whole are fully upheld.
Since confederation and especially since the beginning of the 20th century, this country has known an industrial development unparalleled in its history. From 1900 onwards, our lumber industry, our mines, our waterpower have been developed as never before.
Unfortunately, in several provinces, natural resources were, in most instances, developed only for the benefit of certain foreign companies and, very seldom to the real advantage of our people.
Let us consider, for instance, the forests in my province. Since the turn of the century our forests have been worked on such an extensive scale by pulp and paper companies that, to a certain extent, they have become depleted. At that time, there were no regulations to restrict their activities and, human
1110	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines nature being what it is, these people, whose appetite was never curbed, possessed themselves of all these assets and developed them for their own benefit only, meanwhile forgetting that they were laying waste one of the country's natural resources, one which might take centuries to rebuild.
Fortunately, the Quebec government, in the past few years, realizing this danger, has adopted legislation to save our forests. They have in this way required all those who work our pulp and wood resources to manufacture these products in Canada and to export them in a manufactured or finished state. In doing so, this government showed national consciousness.
This example was followed in several provinces. New Brunswick and Ontario among others, have followed suit and passed similar important legislation. This logical step had been taken for the sole purpose of protecting our forests, the government of the day realizing that they were a national treasure belonging to the population as a whole.
Natural gas is no doubt a different problem but nevertheless we have the power to study a charter which will allow us not only to develop a natural resource but also to export it.
The place we hold today among the exporting countries of the world is incomparable. However we can keep this rank only if we always proceed carefully, if we use our natural resources so that the products of our soil are developed at home and if we apply the principle of Canada first, in this case as in others.
As the leader of our party said the other day, the main reason why we oppose this bill is because we believe in the principle of Canada first. The members of our party were accused of filibustering, and of lengthening the debate but I sincerely believe that when they take such an attitude they are really anxious to carry out their mandate. I am personally glad that they have thus risen in protest and that, as representatives from all the province in Canada, they have put aside any selfish feelings to come to the aid of the people of British Columbia by helping them to secure an adequate and sufficient public service before a group of capitalists export these products to the United States.

APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
In
resuming the debate, Mr. Speaker, on the motion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to establish a joint committee of both houses to give further thought to the social question, I wish to congratulate him again on that move, which will be most helpful to the country. At the outset, I must say that the minister has taken the greatest care to improve health conditions in this country since he has assumed the functions of the head of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I shall try not to repeat what has been said by my colleagues who have spoken on the matter, and I shall also try to consider the whole matter from a human rather than a political point of view. I am assuming, in the first place, that every hon. member of this house desires the well-being and good health of his fellow citizens. That is natural. Let us suppose that a Canadian left this country twenty-five years ago and returned today. He would be astounded at the progress that has been made in social legislation. Twenty-five years ago there was no old age pension; there were no family allowances; there was no pension for needy mothers-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: Good old days!

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
There was no unemployment insurance, and the age of the hon. member for York South was much less than it is now, and it is the same with all of us. There are many social advantages that the people who lived a quarter of a century ago could not benefit from. Now we have made progress in that direction, and although it is impossible to expect perfection in the field of social security, Canada is one of the leading countries in that regard because of the efforts of the Prime Minister and the members of his government, and particularly the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin).
Twenty-five years ago there were government annuities, but they were contributory.

There were some pensions for railwaymen, but they were also contributory. In these last years some benefits have been given that have been non-contributory in order to help the most needy.
I am very much interested when I hear a discussion about contributory social measures. In many instances those who are supposed to benefit from them have not the means to pay any contribution, and there are those who have been deprived of the means of paying any contribution. All hon. members of parliament must be familiar with some of those cases, which are due to poverty and ill health. Now we have the suggestion that a pension be given to invalids. There are hospitals where many invalids could be looked after: those who are fortunate enough to be able to pay for their hospitalization and care, and those who are not so fortunate, and those who through public assistance may go to the hospital and be looked after.
The people of Canada have a natural sympathy for invalids, all those who suffer, particularly and especially disabled persons. But we should not conclude that because a person is disabled he is needy. I knew the greatest lawyer who ever argued before the courts of the province of Quebec. He was disabled; he was a hunchback; nevertheless he was acknowledged as one of the brightest legal minds of Canada. Down home in Riviere du Loup the manager of a furniture factory was also a hunchback, but he had ample means and was the employer of quite a number of people. It is not only the disability that should be the reason for a pension. It should be the disability and the need because of some unfortunate circumstances that are difficult to establish.
It is very difficult to make a distinction between a disabled person who is needy and one who is not. But if the state is to consider these cases, each case should be considered individually. It is impossible to establish general rules in that regard, and probably that is one of the reasons why the disabled have not received a pension.
To what degree is a person disabled? That is the question that must be asked before granting a pension. But nevertheless the disabled deserve our sympathy, whether they are in a position to earn their own living or not. I know well a family where there are five children who are disabled and invalids. The five children are in one family. They are grown up now. They are hunchbacks. They are between thirty and forty years of age. They have been brought up without any help from the state, and I can only admire their parents for having taken care of them for such a long time. They could have gone to hospital
Old Age Security
and they would have been received there, and the cost of their hospitalization would probably have been paid under the public assistance legislation; but the mother and the father loved their children. The father was working to earn their living. The mother was taking good care of them and wanted to have them at home to look after them herself. 1 find it admirable. When it was suggested that they go to the hospital and be looked after by other people, just as is done in many other cases, the mother positively refused, and the children refused. They wanted to be together at home. Well, now, in very pitiable cases such as these it seems to me that these unfortunate people should be granted the same pension that is given to old1 people. In the case of old people it is age. They have the need on account of their age. That is the reason for the means test. The younger people who have suffered a greater disability than those who are old deserve the same consideration; and it would be much cheaper for the state to pay such a pension than to pay for their hospitalization. Considering the wages and the salaries that are paid in hospitals, the medical costs, the fees, the cost of treatment and so forth, it is impossible to look after an invalid and the disabled in a hospital as well as it is done in their homes and at the same cost. It would be much more expensive to look after them in hospitals than in then-homes, if they are given the pension. This is the pension that has been requested for them.
I wish to be fair with those people. I do not tell them that they will have a pension- although I hope they will. I tell them I will never miss an opportunity to bring their cases before the House of Commons so that all hon. members may be made familiar with the circumstances under which they live, and the troubles they have.
In each individual there is an aspiration for justice, and there are cases which strike the imagination of all. We realize that there are family allowances for those under sixteen years of age, and pensions for the blind from the age of forty-

speechtext:
Yes, it is twenty-one now; and I congratulate the minister upon that. We realize that there are old age pensions and that there are pensions for needy mothers with children under sixteen years. This last-mentioned provision is made provincially, through a provincial organization.
Those who suffer disabilities which prevent them from earning their own living look at those people-and not with either envy or jealousy, because people who suffer are as a rule kind. But they will say, "How is it

Old Age Security
that those people who are in no worse condition than we are receive indemnity, while we are deprived of it?" That is the point they consider.
I am deeply concerned when an argument of that kind is advanced by one who suffers. They may be living in the woods or in the back country, far from the railways. They may live alone, deprived of the amenities of life; but they are deserving of our sympathy.
I am not complaining about social legislation, because I realize it was needed. After the exploitation of the forests ceased to be what it was during the war, there were many families who relied upon social welfare grants for their living. A poor woman, the mother of twenty children, wrote me one day stating that, as the mother of twenty children, she was thankful for the establishment of family allowances by the government. That whole family must depend on family allowances. I will not say that this is generous, because in most families the amounts received for family allowances are used in the education of the children, and to dress them comfortably so that they may attend school. All this is in order.
But there are some other cases-and if there were not so many it would be easier to deal with them-who, because of illness, a lack of work or because of some other circumstances, find that they must suffer. There is no reason at all in a country like ours for people suffering from a lack of clothing, or from undernourishment.
I do not wish to discuss this point at length, but during the war I found that there were Canadians who did not have much money, and some of whom were settlers in the back country who did not have sufficient money to buy warm clothing for their children during the winter. The result was that the children had to stay in their camps, instead of going out to play in the snow and to breathe the fresh air. I suggested that secondhand military clothing should be given to them. It was not expensive, and it was at hand, and had been used. For a time I succeeded in getting some of that clothing. I obtained some long overcoats and tunics, the only condition being that they were to be dyed.
On New Year's Eve one winter, in Riviere du Loup, just at the outset of the war, I distributed three hundred of those garments, and sent packages to the back country settlements. But this was stopped by Colonel Ralston and his associate minister under the pretext of economy. What happened? While the white men could not have any more of those garments, the Indians were permitted to have them; and quantities of that clothing were sold at 241 cents a pound to rag pickers.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
Those who were in charge of the colonization offices could not buy them at any price. I tried to buy some and I was told that an order in council would be required. I bring this to the attention of hon. members to show once again the stupidity of some people, and their lack of heart. They did not understand that it was better to give to good Canadians those clothes that had been bought with the money of the Canadian people, and at least as many to whites as to Indians. Instead of that, only the Indians were served, and quantities were sold to rag collectors. Shame!
This was a simple way of furnishing warm clothing during the winter months so as to decrease the discomfort and poverty of certain areas. It is not necessary to have a complicated system and to consult the learned economists and the great social masters about what is done in this or any other country. Perhaps we may learn something from what happens in other countries, but we must consider first what happens in Canada. Those who contend that everybody in Canada is rich cannot be right, because twenty centuries ago our Lord said, You have the poor with you always. I have compassion for the crowd, because that is a condition of existence in this world. Conditions cannot be changed completely but they can be improved. That should be our aim without political partisanship. We should join hands to try to improve the condition of the rather small number of Canadians who need help so that they will be more contented to live in this country. I want my fellow citizens to be happy. These people are not exacting; they do not ask for much. All they are asking for is a kind thought and the consideration that they deserve because they are not able to enjoy the amenities of life that most of us do.
When I meet these people I feel great sorrow and I regret that I am not rich enough to help them. This cannot be done by the individual, it must be done by the state. But if the state does it it means that the money must come from the taxpayers. Those who receive gifts from the state should bow to the taxpayers in thanks. This applies to the youngest child in receipt of family allowances as it does to the centenarian who receives an old age pension; each one should bow to the taxpayer for what is being done for him, and at the same time should not forget that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is his best friend.

I am not a
preacher nor a teacher and I have not had a university education. But I can speak on this subject from some practical experience. Since I was a young man I have been dealing with social services, not at the top level of government but at the lower municipal level. I was elected as a councillor and after serving two years in that position I was elected reeve of our municipality. I served as reeve for six consecutive years before coming here. According to the municipal records of Saskatchewan I was the youngest man ever to hold that office. I do not boast about that, but I am rather proud of it.
While I was municipal reeve I signed thousands of dollars' worth of cheques for social services, to help those who were not able to pay their hospital or doctor bills, to provide supplementary payments to old age pensioners and to those who were getting social aid. This idea of removing the means test in connection with old age pensions would be all right if the needier cases were looked after. I am thinking of those who are crippled, physically unfit, and through no fault of their own not able to look after themselves. I think they come first. Until they are taken care of I believe this talk of removing the means test from the old age pension is nothing but a lot of window-dressing and lip service.
If I may, I should like to refer to a case in my own constituency: In doing so, may I say that I am sure all other members of the house have had the same experience in their constituencies and also in almost all communities. When a municipal official collects taxes, just as the federal government does, to deal with social services, through taxation, they collect the money, make payments to those who are in need, and are never criticized if, in doing so, they provide, with a means test, money for social services to those who need it. It is possible that I might be a member of this house and not be very bright. There are many people who, I believe, are elected to the federal parliament possibly because the organization of the party put them there. But when a man is elected to a municipal council year after year he is running on his own steam.
When I was home at Christmas a man in my constituency asked me to witness a will. I knew him very well, and in speaking to him he brought up the question of the old age

Old Age Security
pension. I said to him that I did not think he needed the old age pension and he said, "No, I don't need it, but I would take it." I do not know exactly how much money he has% but I would suggest it is somewhere around $50,000 in bonds and cash. I said to him that the old age pension would not be any good to him, that he would get it and then he would have to pay it back in income tax. He said, "I am not paying any income tax now; I get enough from the interest on my bonds and the cash to keep my wife and myself." Anyway, he said the income tax would not take much of it.
Then there is another man in my constituency-and there are many such cases- who is a returned soldier. He has a small family and has purchased a farm under the Veterans' Land Act. He is paying income tax. That is all right, but at the same time this returned veteran is keeping his crippled mother. She was paralysed shortly after he came back from overseas, and his father died about the same time. She is bedridden or else in a wheel chair. He is supporting his mother, who is around sixty years of age, and as yet the state has not recognized its obligation to give that woman anything to keep her. I wonder if we would be justified in imposing more taxation on that veteran in order to give pensions to old people who really do not need them. I would like to see the means test broadened. We might get away with it in this house, but if a member of a municipal council handled social services in that way, he would last about as long as a snowball would last in a hot furnace.
I am not going to speak a great deal longer, but there are a few things I should like to say further. Let us keep our social services as a social service. The old age pension is a social service. I commend the minister for introducing the motion to set up a committee to investigate this matter because I think it needs investigation. I am not too surprised at the attitude of the C.C.F. party. They have always advocated something for nothing, but I am a little surprised at the Conservative party and the stand that some of their members have taken on this question. To hear the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) speak on this subject you would think it was as simple as one, two, three; and the same applies to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). I do not know just why they take that stand.

I have the floor. I listened to a lot of your speeches and did not interrupt. The premier of Ontario takes a little different stand. I heard him say over the radio, and it was reported in

the press, that old age pensions were the No. 1 problem of the Dominion of Canada. If it is the No. 1 problem, then it is not as simple as one, two, three. I am rather glad to note that there is at least one man in the Progressive Conservative party who is still speaking with common sense. If anyone is in doubt about where I stand on the question of old age pensions I hope I have made my position clear. My political opponents, if I have any, do not need to worry about the people in my constituency. I will see that they get my speech. A lot of people are worrying about how they are going to answer these .little papers we received from newspapers. I am going to send them a copy of* my speech and let the chips fall where they may. If anyone wants to insult me that is fine. They can say anything they like about me. They can say that I am an enemy of the old people but this is not true. My mother taught me when I was young to respect the aged and I have always done so. I am always mindful of the aged and am perfectly willing to help them any time I can do so.
I am not a poet, but there is a poem, part of which I remember from my school days. I will tell you the story leading up to it. The poem was in the Saskatchewan reader and possibly some members may have read it. There was an old lady who was trying to cross the street. Every time she went to cross the street she had to back up because of vehicles coming along and stopping her. There was a gang of boys farther down the street who were laughing at the old lady and joking about her plight. According to the poem one boy said:
She's somebody's mother, boys, you know;
I will help you across, if you wish to go.
I always remember that any time I am in a crowd. I am most mindful of the aged, and when I have a chance to help them I do so. I am not boasting, but I am rather proud of the fact that two weeks ago Sunday, when we were through curling, my desk-mate let me off at the Chateau Laurier and I was waiting for the bus. I was standing in a crowd of some twenty men and women. I was not out in front. A little old lady came along, passed by some and said to me, "Son, will you help me cross the street?" I said, "Lady, I will be glad to do so." I do not know why she picked me. I do not think I look so kind, but I was watching, and I always do, for some aged person to help if I can.
There always has been a means test with old age pensions, there is now, and there always will be. The minister has introduced

this motion to send the matter to a committee and I hope that the result will be successful. Regardless of whether or not it is on a contributory basis, we will always have a group of people whom we will have to help further and there will always be a means test. There has been a lot of talk about public opinion. I do not think public opinion is too strong on this issue. I believe the people of Canada realize that the government-our friends in the opposition will say it was under pressure, but let that pass- has recognized the fact that we must look after the unfortunate; that, as the saying is, the strong must carry the weak. That will always be the case; but in regard to having this free and that free, or getting something for nothing, I believe this idea is petering out.

speechtext:
think we can say one thing for the hon. member who has just taken his seat; that is, he has the courage of his convictions. I have before me excerpts from speeches made in the House of Commons and the Senate-I suppose I should say "the other place"-in 1926 and 1927 in which I find thoughts very similar to the speech to which we have just listened. Perhaps I might give one quotation. I shall not name the person who made the speech, but it is taken from Senate Hansard for 1926, the year the old age pension bill had passed the Commons and was turned down by the other place:
If this bill passes, the obligation of the children to look after their father and mother and grandmother and grandfather goes by the board ... Is it judicious for us to impose upon our country such socialistic legislation as this-because it is nothing else-when there is no call for it?
The only difference between what this gentleman was saying in 1926 and what my hon. friend said tonight is that this is 1950, and the world has made considerable social progress since 1926. In 1926 many people called the old age pension act socialistic legislation and put the blame for it on the two labour men who were in the house at that time. Tonight, however, there are very few members who would get up in this house and call old age pensions socialistic legislation. Perhaps the prime minister of that day had a better understanding of the social implications of a measure of this kind than the member who has taken his seat. The prime minister at that time was Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, and this is what he said in introducing the measure:
There is need for society to assist in the protection of its members against a condition which simultaneously places burdens upon the worker whose day's work is done, and on the worker whose
Old Age Security
day's work is just beginning. If the young are to be given a fair start in life, the care of the aged should not be their first responsibility.
I think most people would agree with that statement.
Coming to the resolution before us, I am sure it must be very disappointing to a great many people in Canada. The matter of old age pensions has been before the people of this country ever since it first became an issue in 1926, and it became law in 1927. Since I came here twenty years ago there has not been a session when we have not debated this question. It was debated at considerable length in 1931, and if I had time I should like to put on record some of the statements made at that time. This will be a disappointment to a great many people in Canada because they have been looking forward, not to a committee to investigate the abolition of the means test but to the abolition of the means test itself. As a matter of fact the country came very close to having the means test abolished in 1945, when it was included in the proposals made by the federal government to the dominion-provincial conference of that year. I shall read just a short paragraph which appears at page 37 of the proposals of the government of Canada:
As part of the general proposals now put before the conference, it is proposed that the federal government would establish a system of national old age pensions entirely financed and administered by the federal government, and paid at the uniform rate of $30 per month regardless of means to men and women aged seventy and over in all parts of Canada.
Nothing could be clearer than that proposal. The government of the day, a Liberal government, was prepared to abolish the means test for those seventy years of age and over, and there was no question of where the money was to come from. They knew all about that. They knew, because during the war they were able to find all the money required to pay for our war needs. If we can find money to buy guns surely we can find money to look after those who built up this country, the fathers and mothers of those living in this country today.
I have three or four objections to the resolution now before us. In the first place I regard it as merely a stalling action on the part of the government. This idea occurred to the minister himself, and he referred to it. It would be strange if it had not occurred to the minister, because it is a tactic or manoeuvre with which this government is very familiar. In the session of 1943 and 1944 we set up a parliamentary committee to consider a draft bill providing for national health insurance. Perhaps that bill was not brought before the cabinet, and certainly it never received the endorsation of the cabinet, but

Old Age Security
program, financed by contributions based on ability to pay. That is our position. Let me say further that we are opposed to the insurance principle, where each one takes out according to what he puts in. I am opposed to such a system because it is impossible to put it into effect. I am also opposed to it because, out of the incomes the great mass of the Canadian people are receiving individually today they cannot put by, either voluntarily or compulsorily, sufficient funds to take care of the various contingencies, including old age, which they will have to meet sooner or later. They have never been able to do that, and they are not able to do it now.
Let me draw to the attention of the house just a sentence from the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the minister of finance of that time on the operations of the bank for the year 1944. In this paragraph the governor was referring to the sale of victory bonds, five or six issues of which had been sold at that time. This is what he said:
For many Individuals victory bonds and1 war savings certificates purchased during the war period represent the first significant backlog of savings they have ever been able to build up-
That is not the end of the sentence, but the other part is not as important, and each could be a sentence in itself. The other part is:
-and it is apparent that some high-pressure promoters of dubious or worthless securities are attempting to exploit these savings.
We will leave that part out for the moment, and consider the first part of the sentence, where Mr. Towers makes it clear that never before the war were the great masses of our people in this great and rich country able to save anything worth while. But they saved during the war partly because there was full employment, and, partly, because they could not buy certain consumers' goods and, besides, because of compulsory saving.
If the national income were distributed equitably, a contributory system might work; but, as I said before, its administration would be extremely expensive. But the income of the country is not distributed equitably; and any attempt by compulsion to make people who are already living below the standard of health and decency to provide through compulsory contributions for their old age will only intensify their poverty now, and means will have to be taken to make up for the income taken away.
Let me draw to the attention of the house the present position, so far as savings are concerned. The great mass of the people in Canada who had war bonds and war savings certificates have them no longer. The only other savings they have will be
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
cash in savings accounts in the chartered banks. Every year a statement of loans and deposits, both savings and current, as at September 30, is tabled, and every hon. member has access to it. That return gives the number of accounts in the various categories. Those categories are five in number, and constitute (1) deposits of $1,000 or less; (2) deposits over $1,000 and up to $5,000; (3) deposits over $5,000 and up to $25,000; (4) deposits over $25,000 and up to $100,000; and (5) those in excess of $100,000.
I have the figures for 1948 and, with the exception of the fact that the total amount in the savings banks was greater in 1949 than in 1948, there is very little difference. We find that there were 6,605,952 persons who had savings accounts in our chartered banks, to a total amount of $4,048,535,319.
It looks pretty good, when we see that 6,605,952 Canadians have savings accounts. But the savings accounts of $1,000 or less numbered 5,718,549 and aggregate deposits totalling $953,101,895, or about $166 each.

While 5,718,549 persons had $953,101,895 in savings accounts in the banks, we find that 887,403 persons had $3,095,433,424. If those figures mean anything at all, they must mean that the great bulk of the Canadian people have never been able to save enough to take care of a rainy day- and never will, under our present system of distributing wealth.
I said a moment ago that what we should be discussing now is not whether we have old age pensions on a contributory basis, on an insurance basis, with a means test, or without a means test. We should be considering an over-all social security program.
A large number of our unemployed are not covered by any benefit fund. Sick people are not covered; invalids are not covered; medical services are not provided; nor are hospital services, except in one or two provinces.
We have considerable social security services in the country, and it would be folly to deny it. But what we should seek to do is to integrate all of these under one scheme. The reduction in administrative costs alone would justify our doing so. I appreciate that this would require constitutional changes; but we have made constitutional changes before, and we should be prepared to make them again.
In the few minutes left, let me touch upon the question as to how we are going to provide these social services. During his speech the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MARCH 24, 1950
Martin) was good enough to refer to a statement I made in the house last year. If I may do so without seeming to place too much value on my own opinion, I should like to quote four lines from the excerpt read by the minister. They are these:
When we provide social services of any kind we are providing material things such as food, clothing, shelter and services of one kind or another, which must be produced by those who are working.
I think most hon. members will agree with that-that what we are providing for our old people is food, clothing, shelter and certain services. All of these things that our elder citizens will consume in 1950 will be produced in 1950. What they consumed in 1949 was produced in 1949. You cannot save eggs when you are twenty-one to eat when you are seventy. Nor can anybody save anything else. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) put that point quite clearly when he spoke in this debate. I am prepared to go along that far with the hon. member for Peace River and his party, but I cannot stay with them when they maintain that we can transfer the ownership of commodities from one person to another by merely issuing money.
Let us understand our economic system. The various parties to production have claims of ownership on the total value of the production. If all of the production cannot be consumed it is not because there is not enough money put into circulation in the production process; it is because, as I pointed out in the case of the savings account, some people receive more than they are able to consume while a great many receive much less than they are able to consume. The providing of social services is a means of equalizing the distribution of the national income. That cannot be done without taking from those who have more than they need and giving to those who have less than they need. I do not think anyone should be ashamed of taking part in organizing a measure that will perform that service.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) spoke on this matter. I do not see him here tonight but I wish to thank him for the kindly reference he made to myself. When he tried to tell the house how these measures could be financed I felt that either one of us, to use the language of the street, was "nuts". Because of the kind things he said about me I am not prepared to say which one.
I see you are getting uneasy, Mr. Speaker, and I shall relieve your uneasiness right away. May I say to the minister that this resolution is unworthy of this house.

I notice that suggestion has been dropped ever since that time, and it is not now proposed that any plan of this kind may be financed by a poll tax. That poll tax, I may add, was disguised. It was not called by that objectionable name, but was called a registration fee. But it was to be paid by everyone sixteen years old or over; and the Ontario government was by no means the only government to object to that proposal.
When the suggestion was made that the C.C.F. member who raised this point was quite wrong, I could not help recalling a speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is reported as having said at Armstrong on May 20, 1949:
Our objective is health services for all at the expense of the state.

That is clear enough. That was a positive statement, which I presume was supposed to be taken seriously at that time. I grant that most of the other ministers did not go quite that far. On June 16, 1949, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was reported as saying:
The government will do away with the means test for old age pensions.
I emphasize those words. He did not say, "We will appoint a committee to find out if we are going to do away with it, or if it can be done away with." He said the government would do away with the means test. Then on May 28, at Nelson, British Columbia, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), as reported by the Canadian Press, had this to say; and there has been no subsequent amendment of this statement:
Provision of hospital services for the people of Canada and compulsory contributory superannuation are measures expected for the next session of parliament if the Liberal government is returned.
No committee, no inquiry, no doubts! The government knew what it was going to do. May I read it again:
Provision of hospital services for the people of Canada and compulsory contributory superannuation are measures expected for the next session of parliament if the Liberal government is returned.

The Liberal government plans to call a dominion-provincial conference to discuss the establishment of a contributory scheme for old age pensions to start at sixty-five once the election is over and the political heat is done.

That is exactly what the government is not doing. That is exactly what the government is failing to do. Instead of calling a dominion-provincial conference to put into effect a contributory old age pension scheme at the age of sixty-five without a means test, as stated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on June 8, they are appointing a committee to find out whether they should even suggest a plan of this kind. That is exactly what they are now proposing. They want to find out from a committee whether or not what they said then should really be put into effect. Oh, no; it is not the same thing by any manner of means.
This is not anything new, Mr. Speaker, because in 1945, which was the year in which the conference to which I have referred met, in an election which had taken place earlier one of the statements published by the national Liberal committee, in an advertisement put forward under the heading "Just Plain Sense!" is this one, which is No. 9:

speechtext: Oh, there is to be a conference in the fall because the financial agreements come to an end at the conclusion of this coming financial year. That is the only reason there is going to be a conference in the fall. Let there be no suggestion that this is a virtuous proposal by the dominion government. They waited until the last minute. These agreements are running out. There is to be a conference; and the only reason they are calling a conference, which has been demanded ever since the adjournment of the conference in 1946, is that they are obliged to have it in order that there can be new agreements. There is no other reason for it; and no one need expect anything else from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On Monday, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)

will move the motion that appears in his name in Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, March 23, and which reads as follows:
That on Monday, the 27th of March Instant, and on Wednesday, the 29th of March instant, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all business except the introduction of bills, questions and notices of motions for the production of papers.
Without this motion we would spend the day on pipe line bills. On Monday we shall call Bills Nos. 16, 17, 56 and 54. Those are the four bills with regard to which motions were passed yesterday and today; two of the bills are sponsored by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), one by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and one by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. May hew). I understand that if these bills are not passed by both houses of parliament and sanctioned before March 31 the statutes will lapse.
If we were fortunate enough to complete this work we would take up the motion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the motion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that is, the motion on which the debate was just adjourned and the motion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to refer his estimates to the committee on external affairs. If we were a little more fortunate we would take up resolutions No. 4 and No. 9 on today's order paper.
Will the bills be called in the order named by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Bill No. 16, to amend the Agricultural Products Act, and Bill No. 17, to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act, will be the first ones called.
